Registered Office: Charles House, 108-110 Finchley Road, London NW3 5JJ March 2012 Vol 39 No 9 #### CESCO 2012 – Special Issue This issue of **_Copper Studies_** is published to coincide with CESCO Week and CRU’s 11th World Copper Conference held in Santiago, Chile. #### The impact of economic growth in emerging markets on the capital costs of greenfield copper projects _page 2_ In the last decade, economic growth in a number of developing countries, most notably China, has accelerated, thereby generating a significant improvement in the standard of living for many people. New consumer markets have consequently emerged, boosting demand for metals and causing an imbalance between global supply and demand for copper. In turn, this has encouraged investment in new Greenfield copper projects in an effort to ensure that future growth in production keeps pace with increases in world demand. This article analyses the main effects of open market reforms in China on world economic growth and thus on copper demand. It also seeks to highlight the strong relationship between robust growth in copper demand and the high capital costs required to develop and commission new mines.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com
www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES March 2012 2 ###### Introduction The current cycle of world economic growth has see

n nations such as China, India and Brazil experience similar growth rates to those that developed countries had observed in the period of economic recovery after World War II. In Latin America and Asia, millions of people crossed the poverty line and directly engaged in the consumer market. This shift in developing countries has led to huge investment in all types of infrastructure. As a result, consumption of commodities has reached new highs and, despite the recent financial crisis, the trend has continued. This strong demand has caused rapid inflation for major items of mining equipment. Consequently, mining companies face a common problem: the sharp escalation in capital expenditure for the development of mining projects and copper is no exception. 

###### The Sleeping Giant Awakes 

For hundreds of years, Chinese society had relied on rural work, with most of the population closely linked to the land. According to the Chinese National Bureau of statistics (NBS), only 19% of the population lived in cities in 1980. By the end of 2011, however, around 690.8M Chinese people were living in cities, against 656.6M people living in rural locations. Urban dwellers now account for 51.27% of the total population, which is almost 1.35B in total. The table below shows how the population in urban areas has increased during the last three decades. This rapid rate of urbanization has also been responsible for the country’s outstanding economic performance as millions of people have moved to towns and cities in search of better jobs and wages.

Beijing estimates that 300M more people will migrate from rural areas to cities in the next 20 years, thereby sustaining the largest and most rapid urbanization process in history. China’s urbanization rate is equivalent to that of the US in 1910 and Brazil’s position in the 1950’s and Korea’s situation in the early 1970’s. Chart 1 shows the extent to which Chinese and Indian urbanization rates are lagging behind those of other countries. 

The emergence of China as a global economic power is among the most dramatic economic events of recent decades. Although the Chinese economy is beginning to show signs of a deceleration in growth, the process of economic liberalization, initiated by Deng Xiaoping in 1978, cannot be reversed as living standards have already improved dramatically for most of the population. In summary, China’s strategy of development has been based on changes in land use, promotion and expansion of exports, protection of its internal market, promotion of foreign trade and investment, and creation of Joint-Ventures with Chinese state-owned companies in order to invest in heavy industry. As a result, China has moved from a closed, centrally planned system to a more market-oriented one. 

###### China still has a long way

to go to improve the quality of life for everyone After three decades of development, Chinese GDP has grown more than tenfold. In 2010, China overtook Japan and consolidated its position as the second-largest economy in the world. In 2011, Chinese GDP represented around 46% of that in the US and by 2020 this figure is expected to rise to 84%. Meanwhile, Russia and India are set to become the fourth and fifth largest economies respectively. Despite China’s impressive growth rate, GDP per capita remains low when compared to other Asian nations. The fact that per capita income is currently so far behind means that Chinese growth will continue to be boosted by the "catch-up effect" for some time yet. Chart 2 provides a comparison of standards of development for selected developing countries and illustrates that China and India have a long way to go before reaching the standards of development equivalent to their Asian neighbours.  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES March 2012 3 Urbanization Rate

The level of development achieved by the emerging countries has boosted the consumption of mineral resources. In the last decade, these countries were responsible for enhancing growth in demand for metals including copper. Growth in construction activity, transport systems, power and communication networks as well as the rise in demand for consumer durables has represented a significant opportunity for metalproducing countries. In the coming years, the emerging markets will remain the key driver of global economic growth. Average GDP growth is forecast to be 3 times greater in developing countries when compared to mature economies. This scenario highlights the fact that commodities demand from these countries will continue to grow above the world average. ###### New trends for capital costs in mining The strong rate of growth of metal consumption seen over the last decade, driven mainly by the emerging markets, has pushed metal prices to historically high levels. This upward pressure on metal prices, reflecting supply shortages, has encouraged miners to invest massively in new capacity in order to  2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES March 2012 4 balance the minerals and metal industry. If, on the one hand, those projects benefit from strong demand, then, on the other hand, they are affected by capital cost increases. For the most part, capital cost increases can be explained by high metal prices, especially iron ore. In recent years, miners have been complaining that the capital costs for mining equipment have changed dramatically, driven

primarily by the price of steel. Competition for resources such as supplies, labour and services makes the development of a project even more challenging in this booming sector. 

Miners face issues when seeking a labour force to work on project development and implementation. Most deposits are located in remote areas, which makes the recruitment of a team required to work far from home ever more costly. Economic factors, such as exchange rates, also affect project development. For example, the Chilean Peso and the Brazilian Real have strengthened against the US dollar in the last decade and that explains part of the increase in capital costs for new projects in those countries. 

Beyond the technical challenges involved in bringing a new project on-stream, miners have had to take other issues into account. It is already established in the mining industry that companies have to improve conditions in the local communities in which they operate. Most of them have to provide infrastructure and spend money training local workers to operate the facilities. In addition, environmental affairs are becoming more important. Environmental laws are getting stricter, forcing miners to have more consideration for the environment. Nowadays projects have to treat all emissions from mines and plants, which previously were just discharged. 

To illustrate the impact of world economic growth on the capital costs of mining projects, some examples of large-scale projects have been chosen from a vast list of copper projects worldwide.  Relevant data from these operations has subsequently been analysed. In order to ensure that the analysis is comparable between companies, only greenfield sulphide milling projects have been taken into account. 

###### Xstrata’s big challenge 

Xstrata, the fourth largest copper mine producer, has several world class assets in its portfolio to be developed. Moreover, the company is about to complete, at its JV operations, the US$1.3B Antamina expansion and is to go-ahead with the increase in capacity at Collahuasi, for which a feasibility study is underway. It may well be a challenge for Xstrata to develop the whole of its project pipeline both on time and on budget. 

The mining company also aims to develop Antapaccay and Las Bambas (Southern Peru), Agua Rica (Argentina) and Tampakan Project (the Philippines). The first study made on Antapaccay was with the intention of extending life-of-mine at the Tintaya operation. At that time, an investment of US$530M was required to increase copper-in-concentrate production by 100,000t. But in 2008, Xstrata started a feasibility study for a greenfield project rather than an expansion. Preliminary data indicated an investment of US$1.29B for 160,000t of copper-in-concentrate. In 2010, a final study was ready, indicating that Xstrata would need US$1.47B to bring Antapaccay on-stream as a greenfield copper mine. The project was approved by the company’s board and works started immediately. Capital e

xpenditure has not been updated since approval and will remain unknown until construction is complete. 

The capital cost for Las Bambas has shown little variation over time, which might be due to the investment compromise that the company agreed when the Peruvian state granted the project. The first estimation, after the pre-feasibility study update, indicated an investment of US$2.08B to produce an average of 215,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. When the feasibility study was completed (2009), it indicated production of 400,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate with capital costs of US$4.1B. Xstrata approved the project in 2010 with an increase of US$100M in the original budget. 

Xstrata is carrying out a feasibility study for Agua Rica through its subsidiary Minera Alumbrera Ltd. The previous capital cost for the project was US$1.9B for an average production of 150,000t/y of copper-inconcentrate. A preliminary number released by Minera Alumbrera in 2010, suggested that the total

5 

investment for Agua Rica would be US$2.1B. Tampakan is probably the biggest challenge that Xstrata will face in developing copper deposits. This project has to overcome local opposition and constant capital cost increases. Preliminary data indicated an investment of US$2.96B to produce 330,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. The capital required jumped to US$5.2B in the pre-feasibility study in 2009, then to US$5.5B in the feasibility study. The last update stated capital costs of US$5.9B. 

The table on page 6 shows the evolution of unit capital cost increases for projects under analysis. Tampakan had the largest variation, without the final feasibility study even being finished. It is sensible to expect further changes in Las Bambas and Agua Rica. The first one has not been updated for almost two years and construction work is just starting. Unit capital costs of US$10,500/t seem low, even for a greenfield project as big as Las Bambas. Agua Rica may also show a significant increase in unit capital costs when the definitive feasibility study is completed and the project is submitted for internal approval. 

###### Capital costs for Codelco’s MMH have increased by 34% 

Codelco, the world’s top producer, has seen capital costs increase while developing the Mina Ministro Hales (MMH) project. MMH is the first of Codelco’s four main projects to start construction. The other three projects are the new mine level at El Teniente, Chuquicamata underground and the Andina phase II expansion, all of them brownfield projects. In 2008, Codelco completed a prefeasibility study and initial capital costs were estimated at US$1.7B to produce 170 000t/y of copper-in-concentrate at MMH. Immediately a feasibility study was carried out and the project was submitted for approval in 2010. By the time MMH was approved, capital costs had risen to US$2.2B. At the end of 2011 construction

works were 23% complete and total costs were revised to US$2.28B. Further increases will not be a surprise. 

###### Costs for Rio Tinto’s Oyu Tolgoi have risen by US$2B since approval 

Rio Tinto’s largest copper project under construction, Oyu Tolgoi, was approved in 2010 after tough negotiation with the Government of Mongolia, in which the country acquired a 34% share in the project. Rio Tinto became the largest shareholder in late January 2012 after buying shares to increase its stake to 51%. The project started construction in 2010 with estimated capital costs of US$4.6B to produce an average of 410,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. This investment is an update from a previous feasibility study that stated that capital costs for Oyu Tolgoi would be US$3.95B. In September 2011, the project had achieved a 54.4% level of completion. The most recent data indicates that at least US$5.9B will have been spent on Oyu Tolgoi by the end of construction, representing an increase of almost 50% from the feasibility study to final construction. Besides the challenge of implementing the second half of the project on time and on budget, Rio Tinto also has to deal with a new attempt from the national government to negotiate the timeframe within which to increase the Mongolian stake to 50%. According to the contract signed by the parties, the government has the right to increase its stake only after 30 years. 

Capital costs for Pan Pacific Copper’s Caserones project have risen to US$3B PPC’s Caserones Project (Chile), formerly known as Regalito, received approval for construction by the Board on February 2010. At the time the project was submitted, the capital cost in the feasibility study was US$2.0B for an average production of 150,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. That represents an increase of US$300M from 2008’s pre-feasibility study when capital costs were forecast at US$1.7B. Recently, PPC has reviewed the investment to develop Caserones and capital costs increased to US$3.0B, which represents a change of 76.5%. Despite the increase in capital costs, the schedule of implementation has been going ahead as planned. The company started pre-stripping one month earlier than planned. 

###### Output higher at China Minmetals’ El Galeno project but unit costs up 38.6% 

In November 2011, it was reported that China Minmetals’ El Galeno (Peru) project would have annual average production that was 40% higher than originally planned. The company updated a feasibility study that indicated production of 200,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate compared with an earlier mine plan of 144,000t/y. The estimated capital cost for the project is now US$3.85B compared with a previous cost of

The companies are about to start a feasibility study on the capital intensive Galore Creek project after it has been kept under care and maintenance since 2010. Preliminary data from a prefeasibility study estimated that capital costs for the project were US$3.7B. After a pre-feasibility study was completed, total investment was estimated at US$4.15B for copper-in-concentrate production of 134,000t/y. In June 2011, NovaGold Res

ources announced an updated capital cost estimation of US$5.4B, an increase of 45.9% from a previous estimate of unit capital expenditure. 

###### Capital costs increase at Goldcorp’s El Morro project despite the drop in copper production 

El Morro is a world class copper-gold project in Chile in which Goldcorp has a 70% partnership, while New Gold holds the remaining 30%. The project was approved recently by the company and construction will start in September 2012 at a capital cost of US$3.9B for an average production of 129,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. When the feasibility study was completed in 2008, the capital cost was US$2.5B for production of 170,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate. In 2010, El Morro was expected to produce 150,000t/y, after a review in the feasibility study. Unit capital costs increased by 105.6% from the time the feasibility study was completed to the time of the Board’s approval. 

###### Capital costs rise by more than US$1.2B at the Sierra Gorda copper project 

Sierra Gorda is a molybdenum-copper project in Chile, formerly owned by Quadra FNX, and now part of the KGHM portfolio. In September last year, Quadra and Sumitomo closed a JV agreement over Sierra Gorda. When Quadra announced results from the feasibility study, capital costs were US$2.87B for an annual copper-in-concentrate production of 139,000 t/y during the first phase of the project. A previous study estimated capital costs of US$1.66B for the first phase. The current unit capital cost is 73.3% higher than announced before. 

###### Salobo Phase I is about to start production after capital costs rise by 160% 

Salobo, a world class copper-gold deposit owned by Vale and located in Carajбs (Brazil), was discovered in the 1970’s. Since then, Vale has been committed to developing the project, carrying out studies to approve construction. The project was finally approved by the Board in 2007 with capital costs estimated at US$897M to produce 100,000t of copper-in-concentrate per year. After two years of construction, Vale updated capital costs for Salobo to US$1.8B. Meanwhile, Vale approved an expansion at Salobo to double copper production with an incremental investment of US$855M. The expansion is being constructed in conjunction with the first phase of the project. In November, Vale said development of Salobo was 96% complete and production was scheduled to begin in the first half of 2012. The expansion underway is to increase copper production from 100,000t/y to 200,000t/y and is scheduled to be complete in H2 2013. 

###### Conclusion 

Global demand for metals is expected to remain strong, driven mainly by economic activity in emerging markets. The competition for resources when developing new mines will continue to be fierce among mining companies. The effect of this competition to develop copper mine projects can be observed worldwide, although the majority of the projects analyzed in this article are in South America. New greenfield projects are hi

ghly capital intensive and further increases in costs can compromise their competitiveness. Technical challenges to develop a mining project are extremely high these days, so it is imperative that mining companies invest time and money to carry out good engineering studies before board approval to avoid unexpected increases in capital costs during the construction phase.

### CRU and CESCO 

The CRU-sponsored CESCO scholarship scheme is now in its fifth year. Since 2007, CRU has sponsored two or three CESCO Scholars each year to visit London and spend some time with CRU’s Copper Team. During the visit the scholars learn how CRU’s Copper and other teams work. They also visit the London Metal Exchange and head offices of major mining companies in London. Atlantic Copper also sponsors a visit to its head office in Madrid and to its smelter-refinery complex at Huelva. 

Prior and during their visit to CRU, the scholars also research and write articles for **_Copper Studies_** . 

###### About CESCO 

The Center for Copper and Mining Studies, CESCO, is an independent, non-profit organisation created in Santiago in 1984. The members of CESCO work as executives or consultants for national and foreign mining companies, others as professors in local or foreign universities. Throughout its history, CESCO has positioned itself as a meeting place for diverse sectors interested in mining --business, academia, policymakers and professionals-- to promote ideas and discuss criteria about public policies related to economic and mining activities.
